title: What are some obscure horror films that you like?

commenti.body: [removed]
[removed]

The Soviet horror film "Viy" in 1967. Almost the only horror film of the Soviet era.

The classic story is based on. Good actors in the main roles. A leisurely narrative. Folk flavor.

The flight of the little girl in the coffin still scares me a little. Even more devils that appear the next night.

Since you mentioned Ginger Snaps, you may enjoy Kissed (1996) Molly Parker is obsessed with death, so much so that after wandering into a funeral home she wishes to be a mortician. But this fascination becomes highly sexual, as Sandra develops a taste for necrophilia. 

Little Otik (2000) It's based on an old Czech fairytale about a human-shaped tree root that is adopted as a child by parents who can't conceive

Not obscure by any means, but I don't see The Other Side of the Underneath being discussed that much. It really got under my skin when I watched it for the first time, it's like a fever nightmare.

I know Thanatomorphose! It's one of those super obscure horror films, like Absentia, or The 4Bidden Fables. It wasn't bad.
Never heard of it, as I don't watch television.  I find films on my own.

Oh yeah! I got it since I was checking into Noah Taylor. I loved him in Submarine (from the same year). This is quite a different role. I don't look for violent movies and am not the biggest fan of horror films, but I watch any kind of movie if its really good. So I can deal with some violence. But I was shocked by this film. Also from the same director (and qualifying as obscure horror) - Johnny Frank Garrett's Last Word (which I watched a along with a documentary on the same subject).

*The Empty Man* (2020) - it dumped into theaters in the middle of 2020 Covid-19 pandemic with little promotion. But it's the closest thing for someone who wants "H.P. Lovecraft's *The Call of Cuthulu* but set in the midwest."

Does early Cronenberg (let's say pre-Scanners) count as obscure? The Brood, Shivers and Rabid are all wonderfully strange and unsettling. 

While Mandy isn't that obscure, how about Cosmato's 1st film, Beyond the Black Rainbow?

The Reflecting Skin. Such a strange film. I love it and it is rarely mentioned or discussed. A dream like coming of age film, where our young protagonist is living in a dysfunctional world. He becomes obsessed with his neighbor, develops a strange relationship with her, and becomes absolutely paranoid that she’s a vampire. That synopsis is only the tip of the ice berg. I’ve never seen another film like it.

I'm not sure how "obscure" it is, but the incredibly bleak 1971 film _Shura_ by Toshio Matsumoto is fantastic in setting the mood of impending doom, and its use of light and dark (it's almost a chiaroscuro) gets you in an emotional level. 100% recommended.

*Srigala*, an Indonesian partial rip-off/remake of *Friday the 13th* is fantastic and has been on my mind frequently since I saw it months ago. Someone mentioned a Pesce's *Piercing*, but I think his earlier film, *The Eyes of My Mother*, might be obscure enough to recommend here.

>Never heard

Neither had I heard of him either. I don't even own a tv set, but I find films on my own.

I think it has actually found it's audience now, but nobody had heard of The Midnight Meat Train for a long time. It's a 2008 splatter movie based off the story by Clive Barker (Hellraiser, Candyman, Nightbreed, Rawhead Rex etc), was directed by the man behind Godzilla Final Wars and stars (among others) Bradley Cooper and Vinnie Jones.

It's an incredibly thoughtful piece. Genuinely disturbing, loaded with metaphor for city life and clasism, is well acted, written, directed, has great Lovecraft elements and, to top it all off, it delivers and then some on the promised splatter. Like you can go in for all it has to offer, but if you are just a gore hound who wants to see a man get hit on the back of the head with a hammer so hard that his eyeballs fly out, then you can enjoy it on that level alone.

I don’t know how obscure it is these days but The Wailing is generally one of the coolest horror movies I’ve ever watched. Just completely transcendent in terms of tone and build and pay off. I think about it all the time. 

[For anyone who has watched it and wants to understand it better](https://filmcolossus.com/the-wailing-movie-explained/)

The Mephisto Waltz (1971) starring Alan Alda, Jaqueline Bisset, Curd Jügens, and Barbara Parkins.

I think this movie was made to exploit the interest in Rosemary’s Baby. It’s based on a similarly creepy novel but unlike Rosemary’s Baby for better or worse the story was relocated from New York City to LA.

*It Stains The Sands Red* is a zombie movie with (basically) *one* zombie, a *slow* zombie, and it is brilliant and fun and tense. If you like zombie movies, watch it. If you’re bored of zombie movies, watch it.

Kiyoshi Kurosawa's *Cure, Seance* and *Pulse* are supremely unnerving, dread-soaked psychological films that induce horror without using overt horror signifiers.

If you're into Hammer stuff, I'd recommend a lot of the old UK/BBC television plays:

*Nuts in May, Penda's Fen, West Country Tales, Artemis 81, Quatermass, Robin Redbreast, The Shout*, any of the *A Ghost Story for Christmas* instalments (especially if it's an M.R. James adaptation). This sort of horror tends to be far more low-key, slow-burning and rural than a lot of Hammer's output, but collectively seem to transmute the British countryside into its own, eerie character.

“Demon” (2015) is a film that we watched for my weekly film discussion with a group of friends. In this case, my one friend is Polish, and he tends to choose films from Polish directors when he can. I don’t wanna say too much about it, but what I will say is that a lot of horror films use the genre as a means of getting across a metaphor or allegory. Some people have spammed the term “elevated horror” to death, and while I’m not a fan of that description, I would argue that “Demon” uses the genre to illustrate something very personal and disturbing that I hadn’t really seen in any film before that. It’s a short watch, and it’s well worth your time. Probably one of the best horror films of the 2010s. I believe it’s streaming on a couple of platforms rn.

Not sure what your point is or why you're trying to engage me.  I'm not the OP nor was I requesting titles.  But I've already seen all that you listed. You're not as deep or obscure as you seem to thin you are.

The Inferno (1979) by Tatsumi Kumashiro

This is a Japanese supernatural drama film. The horror in this is more on the gothic atmosphere and the dark psychological mood. The director also did erotic 'pink films' and there is plenty of evidence of that in this movie.
The Skin I Live In is excellent

The show Masters of Horror is hot or miss. But the episode John Carpenter's Cigarette Burns is far above the best one. It's a ring-like horror story. Someone searches for a film that causes the audience to go insane. Stars Norman Reedus who is most known for his role as Daryl in the Walking Dead and the film The Boondock Saints.

*The Leopard Man* (1943) is an ensemble murder mystery that prefigures the slasher and giallo genres. It features a few outstanding suspense sequences, snappy dialogue, and superb cinematography.  
  
*A Bell From Hell* (1973) is a Spanish melodrama about a young man who plots his revenge against relatives and acquaintances who may or may not have had him falsely imprisoned.    
  
*The Passion Of Darkly Noon* (1995) is a Southern Gothic thriller about a sexually repressed cult survivor who is taken in by a kind, mysterious woman accused of being a witch.
[removed]

I definitely can vouch for THE BROOD. It is Horror As Metaphor for Family Breakdown ™ to the n-th degree, and it’s one of Cronenberg’s most heartbreaking and human films as far as emotional resonance is concerned. It and A HISTORY OF VIOLENCE and VIDEODROME are my favorite Cronenberg. It’s also one of the most genuinely horrifying and heart-rending and relentless of horror movies IMO.

I love the Shaw Brothers movie Black Magic. It’s kind of a screwball comedy mixed with some pretty disturbing body horror. Love the setting too. Malaysian witch doctors aren’t something I see a lot of in horror. 

The Hammer movie Scream of Fear is also a great one, though more of a psychological thriller. 

Dead of Night might be my favorite anthology horror movie.

Occult (2009) by Koji Shiraishi is a great Japanese found footage horror movie. The special effects aren’t too good, but the movie’s great at creating an overwhelming sense of dread about whether a certain calamity will occur due to the actions of a few characters. This sounds very vague, but that’s because the movie’s best seen completely cold.

My boyfriend introduced me to Cthulhu (2007). Veery obscure, but I think you will find it on Youtube. I loved it, I think it has it's own unique style and it's certainly not going for cheap jump scares.
You’re insufferable
Night Tide, from 1960, stars Dennis Hopper as a sailor on shore leave in a seaside tourist town. He falls in love with a woman who performs as a mermaid in a side show, who may actually be a mermaid.

Martin (1977): utilizing razors and narcotic filled syringes to drink women's blood, a man believes himself to be a vampire

Little Otik (2000): Czech folk tale "greedy guts", one of my favorites because the horror and humor go hand in hand without being forced

Combat Shock (1986): anti-war film about a Vietnam veteran returning home, love the atmosphere in this one - bleak and uncomfortable. a treasure in the genre.

Meet The Feebles (1989): "black comedy musical" but absolutey has a place in horror due to the subject matter, the interactions between the characters, the grittiness and absolute filth of the atmosphere. the characters are anthropomorphic puppets, much like Muppets. one of Peter Jackson's earlier films

Angst (1983): German horror, serial killer is set free from prison and his only desire is to kill again. incredible soundtrack by Klaus schulze as well 

Brain Damage (1988): this one leans toward black comedy, but what a ride. the antagonist is a parasitic worm that feeds on brains and in turn can provide a juice to its host's brain to create an uncontrollable trip-like euphoria, which binds the host to act out the parasite's bidding. could be an analogy for heroin addiction. great movie.

"The Devil's Bloody Playthings." 

Shot on video, with an apparent budget of $25 and some Target gift cards, and I can't remember how I managed to see it -- streaming somewhere, I guess. I haven't found a way to rewatch it and reevaluate it, so it has kind of a mystique for me.

It's a claustrophobic little bit of nastiness taking place entirely in a single room (if memory serves) about a new roommate in the clutches of a sadistic psychopath. It is not good. But it is not good in a very watchable way.

It reminded me of Richard Kern, if Richard Kern didn't have so much talent. But it definitely left an impression, and I definitely want to see it again.

"Jack Be Nimble" NZ horror film I only ever saw once. Very unusual and creepy; NZ has quite a dark streak in their media when you look for it.

"House with Laughing Windows" very Ligotti-esque film. Italian I believe?

"Shadow of the Hawk" '70s Canadian film: a young man is called back to be chief of his tribe but a witch has taken control. Probably not very genuinely First Nations content despite having Chief Dan George in it, but the trailers scared me when I was a kid.
likewise, sweetheart

The horror movie with the most impressive "obscurity to quality" ratio I've seen is **Dark Night of the Scarecrow (1981)**. Thick, foreboding hixploitation atmosphere with an impressive array of legitimately gorgeous shots; at times it almost feels like an oddball cross of 80s B-horror and arthouse cinema. It has a bit of a cult following, but it's not well known at all.

**The Kindred (1987)** is a very well-made body horror sci-fi flick with a creature feature angle. Great practical effects and pretty alright characters. It's kind of bonkers at times, but the scares are serious and good enough to actually be creepy. 

Going full-on obscure, **Deadline (1981)** is a psychological drama/family drama/horror mix about a succesful horror screenwriter with a sinking marriage and a difficult relationship with his kids. It's actually rather serious in tone and is as much a depressing drama as it is a horror movie. It's also pretty meta, the protagonist has to deal with people claiming horror movies are just shlock that pollutes the mind and such.

Gary Sherman's *Death Line* (AKA *Raw Meat*), with Donald Pleasence as the police inspector investigating strange doings in a subway.

Pete Walker's movies have been re-released not that long ago, so maybe getting out of obscurity, but I still don't find too many people who have seen *Frightmare* or *The House of Whipcord*...

Herbert Wise's *The Woman in Black* from 1989.

William Castle's *Shanks* with Marcel Marceau.

Im going to criticize this one. Its very creative and entertaining throughout most of it but in the end failed to fulfill the created expectation.

Felt rushed towards the climax. Ive read that the studio pressured the director to deliver the movie much earlier than what he wanted to. So maybe thats the why.

Still a must see for horror fans. I mean, its good! My criticism is about how much better it could be. Cause its so rare to find real original films.

Let's Scare Jessica to Death (1971) feels like someone got really into Cassavetes then adapted it to a maybe ghost maybe vampire story. It's as spooky as it is heartbreaking and so good!
